name: Electrolytes
kicker: Conduct electricity when dissolved or melted · They break apart into ions
briefing: An electrolyte is any substance that breaks apart into ions when it dissolves in water or melts, so the liquid can carry an electric current. Table salt is a strong electrolyte, the acid in vinegar is a weak one, and sugar is not one at all. Your nerves and muscles depend on electrolytes like sodium and potassium ions, which is why sports drinks advertise them, and every battery needs one between its two electrodes.
answerHtml: Electrolytes (accept electrolyte; accept strong or weak electrolytes; prompt on ionic compounds; do not accept “electrolysis”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Svante Arrhenius’s 1884 doctoral thesis on these substances earned only a low grade at Uppsala, but his theory of how they dissociate in water later won him the 1903 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. That theory explained why their solutions freeze at lower temperatures than expected.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these substances, like table salt, that conduct electricity when dissolved in water because they release ions.

tossups.p: In 1834, Michael Faraday introduced this term along with the words electrode, anode, and cathode. Its name comes partly from a Greek root meaning “loosened,” because Faraday saw these substances break apart when a current passes through them.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these substances, such as salt or acids, whose solutions conduct electricity because they contain ions.

tossups.p: The van ’t Hoff [“vahnt HOFF”] factor of a strong one of these substances is about equal to the number of ions in its formula, about 2 for sodium chloride and about 3 for calcium chloride. That is why they lower water’s freezing point more than the same number of sugar molecules would.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these substances, such as sodium chloride, that conduct electricity when dissolved because they split into ions.

tossups.p: A basic blood test checks the levels of several of these substances, including sodium, potassium, and chloride. In a classic lemon battery, the fruit’s acidic juice serves as one of these substances, letting ions carry charge between strips of zinc and copper pushed into the lemon.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these substances, like table salt, that conduct electricity in water because they release ions.

tossups.p: Debye–Hückel [“duh-BYE HUE-kul”] theory, published in 1923, explains why dilute solutions of these substances behave less than ideally: each ion is surrounded by a loose cloud of oppositely charged ions that partly shields it. That theory calculates the activity coefficients of their ions.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these substances, such as sodium chloride, whose solutions conduct electricity because they contain ions.

tossups.p: Wilhelm Ostwald’s [“OST-vahlts”] dilution law describes how weak examples of these substances break apart into ions more completely as their solutions are diluted. Weak examples include acetic acid and ammonia, while strong examples, like hydrochloric acid, break apart completely.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these substances, like table salt, that conduct electricity when dissolved in water.

tossups.p: When the two wires of a conductivity tester are dipped into solutions, its bulb glows brightly for strong examples of these substances, glows dimly for weak ones such as the acid in vinegar, and stays dark for sugar water. Solid ionic compounds do not conduct, because their ions cannot move until they are melted or dissolved.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these substances, such as salts, acids, and bases, that conduct electricity in water because they break apart into ions.

tossups.p: Car batteries use sulfuric acid as this kind of substance, alkaline batteries use potassium hydroxide, and lithium-ion batteries use a lithium salt dissolved in an organic solvent. Solid-state batteries replace that liquid with a solid that still lets ions move.
tossups.r: Every battery needs one of these between its two electrodes. For 10 points, name these substances that conduct electricity by letting ions move.

tossups.p: In a galvanic cell, a salt bridge filled with a solution of one of these substances, such as potassium nitrate, lets ions flow between the two half-cells so the circuit stays complete. Without that bridge, charge would build up and the current would quickly stop.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these substances, such as table salt, whose solutions conduct electricity because they contain ions.

tossups.p: The hormone aldosterone [“al-DOSS-tuh-rone”] tells the kidneys to hold on to sodium, one of these substances in the blood, and doctors call a low level of sodium in the blood hyponatremia [“hy-poh-nuh-TREE-mee-uh”]. The kidneys keep the body’s levels of these substances steady.
tossups.r: Gatorade was invented in 1965 to replace the water and these substances lost in sweat. For 10 points, name these substances, which sports drinks advertise.

tossups.p: Oral rehydration solution, a simple mix of clean water, salt, and sugar, replaces the water and these substances lost to diarrhea and has saved millions of lives from diseases like cholera. The sugar in it helps the intestine absorb sodium.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these substances, such as sodium and potassium ions, that sports drinks also replace.

tossups.p: In a Downs cell, molten sodium chloride serves as this kind of substance, and electricity splits it into sodium metal and chlorine gas. Calcium chloride is mixed in to lower the melting point, which saves energy.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these substances that conduct electricity when melted or dissolved in water, because their ions can move.

tossups.p: Many hydrogen fuel cells use a plastic membrane such as Nafion as this kind of substance, because it lets protons pass through but blocks electrons. Distilled water barely conducts, so chemists dissolve a little of one of these substances, such as sulfuric acid, in water before splitting it with an electric current.
tossups.r: Seawater conducts electricity far better than fresh water because it is full of these substances. For 10 points, name these substances, like table salt, that release ions when dissolved.

tossups.p: When one of these substances dissolves, water molecules crowd around each ion, pointing their partly negative oxygen atoms toward positive ions and their partly positive hydrogen atoms toward negative ones. Those surrounding clusters of water are called hydration shells.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these substances, such as sodium chloride, whose solutions conduct electricity because they contain ions.

tossups.p: Oxygen sensors in car exhaust systems use a ceramic called zirconia as a solid version of this kind of substance, because oxide ions can move through it when it is hot. Sugar and ethanol, which dissolve as whole, uncharged molecules, are not examples of these substances.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these substances, such as table salt, that conduct electricity when dissolved because they split into ions.

clues.t: Substances that conduct electricity when dissolved in water or melted, because they release ions
Table salt is a classic example; sugar dissolves without making ions, so it is not one
Sports drinks advertise them; the body uses sodium and potassium ions for nerves and muscles
Every battery needs one between its two electrodes
Salts, acids, and bases are all examples
Strong ones break apart into ions completely; weak ones, like acetic acid and ammonia, only partly
Svante Arrhenius’s theory of how they dissociate in water won the 1903 Nobel Prize in Chemistry
Michael Faraday coined the term in 1834, along with electrode, anode, and cathode
A conductivity tester’s bulb glows brightly for strong ones, dimly for weak ones, and not at all for sugar water
Solid ionic compounds don’t conduct, but they do once melted or dissolved, when their ions can move
A salt bridge of potassium nitrate solution completes the circuit in a galvanic cell
Car batteries use sulfuric acid; alkaline batteries use potassium hydroxide
Distilled water barely conducts, so one such as sulfuric acid is added before splitting water with an electric current
They lower water’s freezing point more than the same number of sugar molecules would, which helps road salt melt ice
Arrhenius’s 1884 doctoral thesis on them earned only a low grade at Uppsala
The name comes partly from a Greek root meaning “loosened,” since they break apart
Their van ’t Hoff factor is greater than 1: about 2 for sodium chloride and about 3 for calcium chloride
A lemon battery’s acidic juice is one, letting ions carry charge between zinc and copper; a basic blood test checks sodium, potassium, and chloride
Debye–Hückel theory (1923): each ion in a dilute solution of them is shielded by a cloud of oppositely charged ions
Ostwald’s dilution law: weak ones break apart into ions more completely as they are diluted
Water molecules surround each dissolved ion in hydration shells, with oxygen ends pointing toward positive ions
Gatorade was invented in 1965 at the University of Florida to replace them in sweating football players

Aldosterone tells the kidneys to hold on to sodium; low blood sodium is called hyponatremia
Lithium-ion batteries use a lithium salt in an organic solvent; solid-state batteries use a solid one

trap.title: Not electrolysis!
trap.body: Electrolytes and electrolysis share the same Greek root, and clues about batteries, electrodes, and splitting water fit both. But electrolysis is a process that uses an electric current to drive a reaction, while this answer names the substances whose ions carry that current. Ions are the other trap: electrolytes are the substances that release ions, not the charged particles themselves.
trap.fix: If the question asks for “these substances” that conduct when dissolved or melted, say electrolytes. If it asks for “this process” that splits compounds with electricity, say electrolysis; if it asks for “these charged particles,” say ions.
trap.line: Real answer line: Electrolytes (accept electrolyte; accept strong or weak electrolytes; prompt on ionic compounds; do not accept “electrolysis”)
